name: Apple Design Language rules
author: Edison Augustin X.
description: Enforceable rules for designing apps across the Apple ecosystem, derived from GUIDELINES.md and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines.

rules.title: Prefer standard system components
rules.rule: SHOULD build with standard SwiftUI, UIKit, or AppKit components before customizing, and customize before building from scratch.
rules.why: Standard components adopt Liquid Glass, Dark Mode, Dynamic Type, accessibility, right-to-left layout, and platform behavior automatically.
rules.dont: Rebuild a tab bar, navigation bar, or sheet from primitive shapes.

rules.title: Make actions recoverable
rules.rule: SHOULD build forgiveness in: prefer undo and reversible actions over confirmation prompts, and make guided flows easy to skip or escape.
rules.why: Agency — people explore freely when they know they can reverse an action.

rules.title: Respect systemwide settings
rules.rule: MUST NOT duplicate systemwide settings (appearance, accessibility accommodations, scrolling behavior, authentication) inside the app; the app must follow the person’s system choices.

rules.title: Restore state on relaunch
rules.rule: SHOULD restore the previous state — navigation location, scroll position, window size and position — so people continue where they left off.

rules.title: Work well with multitasking
rules.rule: MUST work with multitasking: save and restore context at any time, pause activities that need attention when people switch away, handle audio interruptions, and finish user-initiated tasks in the background.

rules.title: Name the principle behind non-obvious decisions
rules.rule: SHOULD state which design principle (Purpose, Agency, Responsibility, Familiarity, Flexibility, Simplicity, Craft, Delight) justifies any non-obvious design decision or deviation from a SHOULD rule.
rules.why: Makes agent output reviewable and keeps trade-offs explicit.

rules.title: Don’t decorate in the name of delight
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT add decoration, motion, or effects that get in the way of the task; include only what’s necessary and let every element earn its place.

rules.title: Keep functionality the same everywhere
rules.rule: MUST NOT change the app’s functionality based on the space it occupies or the device it runs on; only the amount of functionality visible at once may change.
rules.do: Move items into an overflow menu or a sidebar as space shrinks or grows.
rules.dont: Drop a feature on iPad because the iPhone layout didn’t fit it.

rules.title: One glossary for every platform
rules.rule: SHOULD maintain a single list of terms and use the same words for the same objects and actions on every platform.

rules.title: Same color meanings everywhere
rules.rule: SHOULD give each color (accent, status, destructive) the same meaning on every platform and use the same accent color.

rules.title: Visually consistent app icon across platforms
rules.rule: SHOULD provide a visually consistent app icon on every platform the app supports so people never mistake it for multiple apps.

rules.title: Same symbols for the same actions
rules.rule: SHOULD represent each action with the same standard SF Symbol on every platform (see ICN-02).

rules.title: Consistent toolbar groupings and placement
rules.rule: SHOULD keep toolbar item groupings and their leading/center/trailing placement consistent across platforms.

rules.title: Consistent search between iPad and Mac
rules.rule: SHOULD keep search placement and behavior as consistent as possible between the iPad and Mac versions of the app.

rules.title: Adapt the container, keep the architecture
rules.rule: SHOULD choose the platform’s own navigation container (tab bar, sidebar, menu bar, vertical tab bar, pages) while keeping the same sections and hierarchy, and keep the layout recognizable and familiar to the platform idiom when windows resize.

rules.title: Give every platform the same care
rules.rule: SHOULD design, preview, and test on every supported platform and configuration (size classes, localizations, text sizes, appearances) instead of porting one platform’s layout.

rules.title: Match context menu actions to swipe actions
rules.rule: SHOULD surface the same top actions in an item’s context menu as in its swipe actions.

rules.title: Decide layout from size classes, not device or orientation
rules.rule: MUST base layout decisions on horizontal/vertical size classes and available space, not on device type (idiom), screen bounds, or orientation.
rules.dont: Branch on `UIDevice.current.userInterfaceIdiom`, `UIScreen.main.bounds`, or `UIDevice.current.orientation` to pick a layout.

rules.title: Respect safe areas and layout guides
rules.rule: MUST keep controls and essential content inside system safe areas, margins, and layout guides; only full-bleed backgrounds may extend beyond them.
rules.why: Hardware features (Dynamic Island, camera housings, reserved regions) and system bars must never obscure content.

rules.title: Adapt to every size-class combination
rules.rule: MUST produce a usable layout for every combination of compact/regular width and height, arbitrary window sizes (iPad, Mac, visionOS, iPhone Duo), external displays, and Display Zoom — without fixed widths tied to one screen.

rules.title: Make layout respond to text size
rules.rule: MUST adapt layout to larger text: stack horizontally adjacent views vertically, let rows grow in height, allow multiple lines, and reduce column counts at accessibility sizes.

rules.title: Order content by importance
rules.rule: SHOULD place the most important content near the top and leading side, following reading order.

rules.title: Align, indent, and group deliberately
rules.rule: SHOULD align related elements, use indentation to show subordination, and group related items with negative space, container shapes, or separators.

rules.title: Use progressive disclosure
rules.rule: SHOULD reduce initial content with disclosure controls, menus, nested views, or scrollable sections instead of showing every option at once.

rules.title: Separate controls from content with Liquid Glass
rules.rule: MUST distinguish controls from content by placing them in the Liquid Glass layer and using a scroll edge effect — not by adding solid or semi-opaque backgrounds beneath controls.

rules.title: Extend backgrounds beneath bars
rules.rule: SHOULD extend full-screen background content beneath sidebars, toolbars, and tab bars; use a background extension effect when a sidebar or inspector would cover important imagery.

rules.title: Scale artwork, never distort it
rules.rule: SHOULD scale background artwork to fill the display when the aspect ratio changes, never stretching it or changing its aspect ratio.

rules.title: Nest corners concentrically
rules.rule: SHOULD give custom components corner radii that are concentric with their container (bars, sheets, windows, hardware), using the system concentric shape APIs.

rules.title: macOS: keep critical items off the window bottom
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT place controls or critical information at the bottom of a window or sidebar, or behind the camera housing.

rules.title: tvOS: honor the safe area
rules.rule: MUST inset primary content 60 pt from the top and bottom and 80 pt from the sides of the screen.

rules.title: tvOS: use grid specifications
rules.rule: SHOULD use 40 pt horizontal spacing and at least 100 pt vertical spacing in grids, with Apple’s unfocused content widths (2-col 860 pt … 9-col 160 pt), consistent spacing, and symmetric partially hidden items.

rules.title: visionOS: space interactive items for eyes
rules.rule: SHOULD place interactive items so their centers are at least 60 pt apart (or keep at least 16 pt of space around each), so the hover effect never crowds neighbors.

rules.title: watchOS: limit controls per row
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT place more than three glyph buttons or two text buttons side by side.

rules.title: No Liquid Glass in the content layer
rules.rule: MUST NOT apply Liquid Glass to content-layer elements such as app backgrounds, list rows, or cards; use standard materials there. Exception: transient interactive elements (slider and toggle knobs) that take on glass while being manipulated.

rules.title: Use custom glass sparingly
rules.rule: SHOULD rely on standard components for Liquid Glass and apply custom glass effects only to the few most important functional elements.

rules.title: No glass on glass
rules.rule: MUST NOT layer Liquid Glass elements on top of each other or overcrowd them; keep standard spacing metrics.

rules.title: Remove custom bar and sheet backgrounds
rules.rule: SHOULD remove custom backgrounds and tints from navigation bars, tab bars, toolbars, split views, sheets, and popovers so the system can render Liquid Glass and scroll edge effects.
rules.dont: Set opaque `UINavigationBarAppearance` backgrounds, `.toolbarBackground(...)` colors, or visual effect views inside popovers.

rules.title: Choose the right glass variant
rules.rule: MUST use the regular variant by default and for text-heavy components; use the clear variant only over visually rich media, adding a 35% dark dimming layer when the content underneath is bright.

rules.title: Test glass with accessibility and display settings
rules.rule: MUST verify custom glass, colors, and animations with Reduce Transparency, Increase Contrast, Reduce Motion, and the person’s preferred Liquid Glass look.

rules.title: Use scroll edge effects correctly
rules.rule: SHOULD use a scroll edge effect only where scrolling content passes behind floating UI, apply one per view (one per pane in split views, with matching heights), and prefer the automatic style.

rules.title: Group custom glass in a container
rules.rule: SHOULD combine multiple custom glass effects inside one `GlassEffectContainer` for rendering performance and fluid morphing, applying `glassEffect` after other appearance modifiers.

sources.title: Applying Liquid Glass to custom views

rules.title: Color on glass: only the primary action
rules.rule: MUST NOT tint the backgrounds of multiple controls; reserve color on Liquid Glass for status or the primary action, and tint its background rather than its symbol or text.

rules.title: Vibrant colors on standard materials
rules.rule: MUST use system vibrant label, fill, and separator colors on standard materials; choose materials by semantic purpose; avoid quaternary label vibrancy on thin and ultra-thin materials.

rules.title: visionOS: keep the glass window background
rules.rule: SHOULD retain the system glass background of windows and prefer translucency over opaque color.

rules.title: Use system colors through their APIs
rules.rule: MUST NOT hard-code system or semantic color values in views; reference them through the system API (`Color.blue`, `Color(.label)`, `UIColor.systemBackground`, `NSColor.labelColor`) or a named asset-catalog Color Set.
rules.why: Apple documents values for design reference only; they change between releases and adapt to appearance and accessibility settings.
rules.dont: `Color(red: 0, green: 0.53, blue: 1)`, `UIColor(hex:)`, `#colorLiteral(...)`, raw hex in view code.

rules.title: Give every custom color all its variants
rules.rule: MUST define each custom color with light and dark variants, each with an increased-contrast option — even if the app ships in one appearance.

rules.title: Never rely on color alone
rules.rule: MUST NOT use color as the only way to convey information, interactivity, status, selection, or focus; pair it with text, shape, or a symbol.

rules.title: One meaning per color
rules.rule: MUST NOT use the same color to mean different things (for example, an interactive tint also applied to non-interactive text).

rules.title: Don’t repurpose semantic colors
rules.rule: MUST NOT redefine dynamic system colors’ meanings — for example, separator as text color or secondary label as a background.

rules.title: Meet contrast minimums
rules.rule: MUST meet at least 4.5:1 contrast for text up to 17 pt and 3:1 for text 18 pt and larger or bold, in both appearances; strive for 7:1 for custom foreground/background pairs in small text. If defaults can’t meet this, MUST provide a higher-contrast scheme when Increase Contrast is on.

rules.title: Follow the system appearance
rules.rule: MUST NOT offer an app-specific appearance setting or force a color scheme; support light, dark, and Auto. Rare exception: immersive media experiences may stay permanently dark.
rules.dont: Apply `.preferredColorScheme(.light)` or `overrideUserInterfaceStyle` to the whole app.

rules.title: Prefer system background colors
rules.rule: SHOULD use the system background set (or the grouped set for grouped tables and forms) at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels so the system can switch between base and elevated colors in Dark Mode.

rules.title: Apply the accent color judiciously
rules.rule: SHOULD reserve the brand/accent color for primary actions, status indicators, and selection (such as the selected tab), and move broader brand color into the content layer.

rules.title: Keep bars legible over colorful content
rules.rule: SHOULD prefer monochromatic toolbars and tab bars over colorful content, avoid control label colors similar to content colors, and keep the resting state (top of scroll) legible.

rules.title: Tame white images in Dark Mode
rules.rule: SHOULD slightly darken content images with white backgrounds in Dark Mode, and provide separate light/dark icon or image assets when one asset doesn’t work in both.

rules.title: Manage color spaces
rules.rule: SHOULD embed color profiles in images, and when using Display P3 provide sRGB variants where colors or gradients would clip or become indistinguishable.

rules.title: Consider cultural color meaning
rules.rule: SHOULD verify that colors communicate the intended meaning in every locale the app supports.

rules.title: Use system color pickers
rules.rule: SHOULD use the system color picker (`ColorPicker`, color wells) when people choose colors.

rules.title: Use built-in text styles
rules.rule: MUST set text with system text styles (`.largeTitle` … `.caption2`) so it supports Dynamic Type and larger accessibility sizes; fixed point sizes that don’t scale are not allowed.

rules.title: Never go below the platform minimum size
rules.rule: MUST NOT display text smaller than the platform minimum (11 pt iOS/iPadOS, 10 pt macOS, 23 pt tvOS, 12 pt visionOS and watchOS), for system or custom fonts.

rules.title: Avoid light font weights
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT use Ultralight, Thin, or Light weights for interface text; prefer Regular, Medium, Semibold, or Bold, and enlarge thin custom fonts.

rules.title: Don’t embed system fonts
rules.rule: MUST NOT bundle San Francisco or New York font files in an app or web page; access system fonts through `Font.Design` (`.default`, `.serif`, `.rounded`, `.monospaced`) or, on the web, the `system-ui` / `ui-serif` / `ui-rounded` / `ui-monospace` families.

rules.title: Custom fonts must scale and respect Bold Text
rules.rule: MUST make custom fonts legible at recommended sizes and implement Dynamic Type (for example `Font.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` or `UIFontMetrics`) and Bold Text support.

rules.title: Minimize typefaces
rules.rule: SHOULD minimize the number of typefaces; when branding requires a custom font, use it for headlines and subheadings and the system font for body and captions.

rules.title: Preserve hierarchy at every text size
rules.rule: SHOULD express hierarchy with weight, size, and color, keep that hierarchy intact as text size changes, and keep primary elements near the top at large sizes.

rules.title: Minimize truncation
rules.rule: SHOULD show as much useful text at the largest accessibility size as at the largest standard size; avoid single-line limits and truncation in scrollable regions unless people can open the full content.

rules.title: Scale meaningful icons with text
rules.rule: SHOULD enlarge interface icons that carry meaning as the text size grows (SF Symbols scale automatically).

rules.title: Prioritize what grows
rules.rule: SHOULD prioritize enlarging the content people care about rather than every string (for example, not tab titles or transient values).

rules.title: Avoid tight leading for long text
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT use tight leading for three or more lines of text; use loose leading for wide columns and long passages.

rules.title: Use platform text style tables
rules.rule: SHOULD match the platform’s built-in text style specifications (e.g., iOS Body 17/22 pt, macOS Body 13/16 pt, tvOS Body 29/36 pt, watchOS Body 16/18.5 pt) when mocking up or implementing custom type.

rules.title: visionOS: keep text flat, bold, and facing people
rules.rule: SHOULD prefer 2D text, maximize contrast with its background, make free-floating text bold instead of adding shadows, and billboard labels attached to 3D objects.

rules.title: Prefer SF Symbols for interface icons
rules.rule: SHOULD use SF Symbols for interface icons wherever a suitable symbol exists; create a custom symbol from an exported template when none does.

rules.title: Use standard icons for standard actions
rules.rule: SHOULD use Apple’s standard symbols for common actions — e.g., Share `square.and.arrow.up`, Copy `document.on.document`, Delete `trash`, Add `plus`, More `ellipsis`, Search `magnifyingglass`, Filter `line.3.horizontal.decrease`, Done `checkmark`, Cancel `xmark`.

rules.title: Keep interface icons visually consistent
rules.rule: MUST give all interface icons a consistent size, level of detail, stroke weight, and perspective, and SHOULD match icon weight to adjacent text.

rules.title: Ship custom icons as vectors
rules.rule: MUST provide custom interface icons as vector PDF/SVG or custom SF Symbols (not single-resolution PNGs), optically centered with any needed padding baked into the asset.

rules.title: Pick the right rendering mode and variant
rules.rule: SHOULD choose a symbol rendering mode (monochrome, hierarchical, palette, multicolor) that stays legible in context; use outline variants in toolbars and lists, fill variants for iOS tab bars, swipe actions, and selection, and slash variants for unavailable states.

rules.title: Variable color means change, not depth
rules.rule: MUST NOT use variable color to convey depth; use it only for values that change (level, strength, progress) and use hierarchical rendering for depth.

rules.title: Animate symbols with purpose
rules.rule: SHOULD apply symbol animations (Bounce, Pulse, Replace, Draw On/Off, etc.) judiciously, only when each communicates a clear meaning consistent with the app’s tone.

rules.title: No custom selected states for standard bars
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT supply selected-state icon variants for standard toolbars, tab bars, and buttons — the system renders selection.

rules.title: Build app icons from unmasked layers
rules.rule: MUST provide app icon layers unmasked at the platform canvas size — 1024×1024 px square (iOS, iPadOS, macOS, visionOS), 1088×1088 px square (watchOS), 800×480 px rectangle (tvOS) — and let the system apply the mask; compose iOS/iPadOS/macOS/watchOS icons in Icon Composer.

rules.title: Consistent icon across appearances
rules.rule: MUST keep the app icon’s core features the same in default, dark, clear, and tinted appearances; base the dark icon on the light icon.

rules.title: Keep app icons simple
rules.rule: SHOULD design app icons around one simple concept with minimal shapes and a simple background; prefer illustrations to photos; avoid replicating UI or screenshots; include text only when essential (never “Watch”, “Play”, “New”, “For visionOS”).

rules.title: Let the system add icon effects
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT bake highlights, shadows, bevels, blurs, or glows into app icon layers; if custom effects are essential, use them intentionally and test them in Icon Composer and on device.

rules.title: Platform-specific app icon constraints
rules.rule: SHOULD keep a safe zone in tvOS icons, avoid hole-like shapes in visionOS background layers, and avoid black backgrounds in watchOS icons.

rules.title: Provide high-resolution image assets
rules.rule: MUST provide bitmap assets at every required scale factor — iOS @2x and @3x; iPadOS and watchOS @2x; macOS and tvOS @1x and @2x; visionOS @2x or higher (prefer vectors) — with embedded color profiles.

rules.title: Add motion only with purpose
rules.rule: SHOULD add motion only when it supports the experience (status, feedback, instruction), keeping feedback animations brief and precise.

rules.title: Respect Reduce Motion
rules.rule: MUST reduce automatic and repetitive animation when Reduce Motion is on: tighten springs, track gestures directly, avoid z-axis depth animation, replace x/y/z transitions with fades, and avoid animating into or out of blurs.

rules.title: Motion is never the only channel
rules.rule: MUST supplement any information conveyed through motion with text, haptics, or audio — motion is never the only channel.

rules.title: Let people cancel motion
rules.rule: MUST keep animations interruptible so people never have to wait for one to finish before acting.

rules.title: Don’t animate frequent interactions
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT add custom motion to UI interactions that happen frequently; system components already animate subtly.

rules.title: Make feedback motion realistic
rules.rule: SHOULD make motion follow people’s gestures and expectations — a view revealed by sliding down dismisses by sliding up, not sideways.

rules.title: visionOS: protect visual comfort
rules.rule: SHOULD avoid motion at the edges of the field of view, fade objects to relocate them, never rotate the virtual world, give a stationary frame of reference, make large moving objects translucent or low contrast, and avoid sustained oscillation (especially near 0.2 Hz).

rules.title: Games: steady frame rate
rules.rule: SHOULD keep games at a consistent 30–60 fps by default on each platform and let people trade visual quality for performance or battery life.

rules.title: Use system haptics for their documented meanings
rules.rule: MUST use system haptic patterns (notification, impact, selection on iOS; alignment, level change, generic on macOS; notification, up, down, success, failure, retry, start, stop, click on watchOS) only for their documented meanings.

rules.title: Consistent, complementary, sparing, optional
rules.rule: SHOULD tie each haptic to one cause, match its intensity and sharpness to the accompanying visuals and sound, prefer short haptics for discrete events, avoid overuse, and let people turn haptics off.

rules.title: Pair audio cues with haptics and visuals
rules.rule: SHOULD pair audio cues with matching haptics and visual indicators for people who can’t hear or have audio off.

rules.title: Don’t disrupt sensors
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT play haptics that disturb camera, gyroscope, or microphone use.

rules.title: Size controls for every input
rules.rule: MUST give every tappable or clickable control a hit region of at least the platform default size (44×44 pt on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS; 60×60 pt on visionOS; 28×28 pt on macOS; 66×66 pt on tvOS) and never smaller than the platform minimum.

rules.title: Space controls apart
rules.rule: SHOULD leave about 12 pt of padding around bezeled elements and about 24 pt around the visible edges of non-bezeled elements.

rules.title: Label every control for VoiceOver
rules.rule: MUST give every key interface element — especially icon-only buttons, toolbar items, and custom controls — a descriptive accessibility label, and keep labels current as content changes.

rules.title: Describe meaningful images, hide decorative ones
rules.rule: MUST provide descriptions for meaningful images and infographics and exclude purely decorative images from assistive technologies.
rules.do: `Image(decorative:)`, `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, `alt=""` for decorative web images; real descriptions otherwise.

rules.title: Let people enlarge text
rules.rule: SHOULD let people enlarge text by at least 200% (140% on watchOS), ideally through Dynamic Type; on the web, never disable browser zoom.

rules.title: Offer alternatives to gestures
rules.rule: MUST make every gesture-driven action also available through an on-screen control (for example, a button as well as swipe-to-dismiss), and use the simplest gesture for frequent actions.

rules.title: Support keyboard-only use
rules.rule: SHOULD let people navigate and operate the whole app with Full Keyboard Access, and support Voice Control, Switch Control, AssistiveTouch, and Pointer Control with properly labeled elements.

rules.title: Structure content for navigation
rules.rule: SHOULD give each screen a unique title, mark section headings, group related elements, set a logical reading order, announce content and layout changes, and support the VoiceOver rotor.

rules.title: Avoid timed interfaces
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT auto-dismiss views or controls on a timer; prefer explicit dismissal.

rules.title: Let people control media
rules.rule: MUST provide discoverable controls to start and stop any audio or video, avoid autoplay without controls, and respond to the Dim Flashing Lights setting in video playback.

rules.title: Provide text alternatives for media
rules.rule: SHOULD provide captions, subtitles, audio descriptions, or transcripts as appropriate, with customizable presentation.

rules.title: Optimize for Assistive Access
rules.rule: SHOULD, when Assistive Access is on, show core functionality only, one interaction per screen, and confirm hard-to-undo actions twice.

rules.title: Audit with Accessibility Inspector
rules.rule: SHOULD audit every screen with Accessibility Inspector and test with VoiceOver, the largest accessibility text size, Increase Contrast, Reduce Transparency, and Reduce Motion before shipping.

rules.title: visionOS: keep people comfortable
rules.rule: SHOULD keep UI within the field of view (prefer horizontal layouts), never anchor content to the wearer’s head, reduce animation speed and intensity in the periphery, and minimize large or repetitive gestures.

rules.title: Games: offer difficulty accommodations
rules.rule: MAY let players customize difficulty, reaction time, or control assistance.

rules.title: Label actions with verbs
rules.rule: SHOULD label buttons and action menu items with a verb or verb phrase (“Send”, “Add to Cart”) and avoid cute or clever labels (“Let’s do it!”).

rules.title: Write descriptive link text
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT use “Click here” or similar vague link text; describe the destination (“Learn more about UX writing”).

rules.title: Describe gestures correctly for the device
rules.rule: MUST use the gesture word that matches the device — “tap” for touch, “click” for pointer — or the device-neutral “choose” where the input method varies (as in alerts).

rules.title: Apply capitalization consistently
rules.rule: SHOULD use title-style capitalization for buttons, menu items and titles, segment labels, column headings, and list/form section headers, and sentence-style for messages, descriptions, and purpose strings — consistently per element type.

rules.title: Use an ellipsis when more input is needed
rules.rule: SHOULD append an ellipsis (…) to menu items and buttons whose action requires more input before completing (e.g., “Rename…”, “Export As…”).

rules.title: Address people directly, avoid “we”
rules.rule: SHOULD address people as “you” (not “the user”), avoid “we” in interface copy, and use possessives like “my” and “your” sparingly and consistently.

rules.title: Write helpful error messages
rules.rule: SHOULD show errors next to the problem, without blame, stating how to fix it (“Choose a password with at least 8 characters”); avoid “Oops!” and robotic messages like “Invalid name”.

rules.title: Give empty states a next step
rules.rule: SHOULD explain what to do next on empty screens and offer a button or link to do it, without placing crucial information there.

rules.title: Use plain, inclusive language
rules.rule: SHOULD write concise, plain language without jargon, undefined technical terms, colloquialisms, or unnecessary gender references, and consider humor carefully.

rules.title: Keep multistep language consistent
rules.rule: SHOULD start flows with language like “Get Started”, advance with one consistent term (“Continue” or “Next”), and finish with “Done”.

rules.title: Label fields and show hints
rules.rule: SHOULD give every text field a label and a placeholder hint (“name@example.com”), and don’t rely on placeholder text alone since it disappears while typing.

rules.title: Keep settings labels practical
rules.rule: SHOULD label settings plainly, describe what happens when a setting is on, and link directly to a setting rather than describing its location.

rules.title: Represent people inclusively
rules.rule: SHOULD use gender-neutral figures, portray diverse people without stereotypes, write about disability people-first, and offer inclusive options (nonbinary, self-identify, decline to state) if gender is required.

rules.title: Internationalize everything
rules.rule: SHOULD externalize all user-facing strings, let the system format dates, times, numbers, and currency, and allow for text expansion.

rules.title: Mirror directional UI in right-to-left
rules.rule: SHOULD flip progress controls, sliders, back/forward navigation, and icons that depict text or forward motion in RTL contexts, and reverse numerals that show progress or sequence.

rules.title: Never mirror what must stay fixed
rules.rule: MUST NOT reverse the digits within a number or flip logos, universal marks (such as the checkmark), photos, or controls that refer to an actual direction.

rules.title: Align text by context and language
rules.rule: SHOULD align one- and two-line text to the interface direction, align paragraphs (three or more lines) to their own language, align all list items consistently, and enlarge Arabic or Hebrew about 2 pt beside uppercase Latin text.

rules.title: Keep text out of images
rules.rule: SHOULD avoid text in icons, images, and launch screens; localize any characters that must appear in an icon.

rules.title: Tab bars navigate; they never act
rules.rule: MUST NOT use a tab bar item to perform an action (compose, add, share); tab bars switch between top-level sections — use a toolbar for actions.

rules.title: Keep the tab bar visible
rules.rule: MUST keep the tab bar visible as people navigate within sections; only a modal view may cover it.

rules.title: Never disable or hide tabs
rules.rule: MUST NOT disable or hide tab bar items when their content is unavailable; show the section and explain why it’s empty.

rules.title: Keep tabs few and labeled
rules.rule: SHOULD use only as many tabs as needed, avoid the overflow More tab, give each tab a single-word label and a filled SF Symbol, and default to five or fewer tabs when tabs are customizable.

rules.title: Reserve badges for critical information
rules.rule: SHOULD show badges on tabs only for new or updated information that warrants attention.

rules.title: Use the platform’s navigation container
rules.rule: SHOULD use the floating bottom tab bar on iPhone; a top tab bar (optionally `sidebarAdaptable`) on iPad; a sidebar or split view plus the menu bar on Mac; the vertical leading tab bar in visionOS windows; the top tab bar on tvOS; and lists or vertical pages on watchOS.

rules.title: Keep sidebars shallow and discoverable
rules.rule: SHOULD show no more than two levels of hierarchy in a sidebar (add a content list in a split view for deeper data), let people customize and hide it with familiar interactions, and not hide it by default.

rules.title: Highlight the path in split views
rules.rule: SHOULD persistently highlight the selection in each pane that leads to the detail view, use split views only in regular width on iPhone, and support narrow, compact, and intermediate widths on iPad.

rules.title: Use the standard Back and Close buttons
rules.rule: MUST NOT replace the standard Back and Close buttons with text labels reading “Back” or “Close”; use the system buttons and symbols (or custom versions that look and behave identically).

rules.title: Write useful, short titles
rules.rule: MUST NOT title windows or views with the app name; use a word or short phrase (under 15 characters) that describes the current content.

rules.title: One prominent toolbar action, on the trailing side
rules.rule: MUST specify at most one prominent primary action (such as Done or Submit) in a toolbar and place it on the trailing side.

rules.title: Group toolbar items deliberately
rules.rule: SHOULD group toolbar items by function and frequency into at most three groups, keep navigation and critical actions in distinct familiar groups, separate text-labeled buttons with fixed space, and not mix text and icons within one group.

rules.title: Prefer borderless system symbols in toolbars
rules.rule: SHOULD use recognizable, borderless system symbols for toolbar items (text only for actions like Edit that symbols don’t represent well), and hide an item itself rather than its contents.

rules.title: Let the system manage toolbar overflow
rules.rule: MUST NOT add a manual overflow menu in iPadOS or macOS toolbars (the system adds one), and SHOULD avoid layouts that overflow by default; add a More menu only for genuinely secondary actions.

rules.title: Use large titles on iOS
rules.rule: SHOULD use large titles that collapse into standard titles on scroll to keep people oriented.

rules.title: Place search where the platform expects it
rules.rule: SHOULD place iOS search as a search tab (`Tab(role: .search)`), in a bottom toolbar when there’s room, in the top toolbar when bottom content must stay visible, or inline above the list it filters; on iPad and Mac, at the trailing end of the toolbar or top of the sidebar.

rules.title: Make search responsive and scoped
rules.rule: SHOULD use informative placeholder text, search as people type, show recent and suggested searches, rank the most relevant results first, and offer scope bars (defaulting to the broadest scope) and tokens.

rules.title: At most two prominent buttons per view
rules.rule: SHOULD give the most likely action a prominent style and keep prominent buttons to one or two per view.

rules.title: Distinguish choices by style, not size
rules.rule: SHOULD present a set of options as equally sized buttons and highlight the preferred one with a more prominent style.

rules.title: Custom buttons need a press state
rules.rule: MUST give every custom button a visible press (highlighted) state.

rules.title: Never make a destructive button primary
rules.rule: MUST NOT assign the primary (default) role to a button that performs a destructive action, even if it’s the most likely choice.

rules.title: Assign semantic button roles
rules.rule: SHOULD assign system roles — primary for the most likely nondestructive action, cancel for canceling, destructive for data-destroying actions — so the system applies accent or red styling and Return/Escape behavior.

rules.title: Use modality only with clear benefit
rules.rule: SHOULD present content modally only when it helps people focus or make a critical choice, keep modal tasks short with a single path, and title the modal view with its task.

rules.title: One modal presentation at a time
rules.rule: MUST NOT display more than one alert at a time, and SHOULD NOT stack sheets, popovers, or other modal views — dismiss one before presenting the next.

rules.title: Always provide an obvious dismissal
rules.rule: MUST give every modal view an obvious way to dismiss it using platform conventions, and confirm before dismissal would discard user-generated content.

rules.title: Pair Done with Cancel or Back
rules.rule: SHOULD pair a sheet’s Done button with Cancel (or Back in multistep flows), place Cancel on the leading edge and Done on the trailing edge on iOS/iPadOS, and avoid showing Cancel, Done, and Back together.

rules.title: Resizable sheets behave like the system
rules.rule: SHOULD include a grabber in resizable sheets, support the medium detent for progressive disclosure when useful, support swipe to dismiss (confirming with an action sheet if changes are unsaved), and prefer page or form sheet styles on iPad.

rules.title: Use alerts sparingly
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT show alerts that are merely informational, appear at launch, or confirm common undoable actions; reserve alerts for critical, actionable information.

rules.title: Write specific, short alerts
rules.rule: MUST limit alerts to a title, optional short message, and at most three buttons; the title MUST describe the situation specifically (never just “Error”) in no more than two lines.

rules.title: Title alert buttons with outcomes
rules.rule: SHOULD title alert buttons with one- or two-word verbs describing the result, use “OK” only in purely informational alerts, never use “Yes”/“No”, always title the cancel button “Cancel”, never make Cancel the default, and place the default button on the trailing side (or top of a stack).

rules.title: Use destructive styling precisely
rules.rule: SHOULD apply the destructive style only to destructive actions people didn’t deliberately choose, and include a Cancel button whenever an alert offers a destructive action.

rules.title: Action sheets for choices about an intentional action
rules.rule: SHOULD use an action sheet (confirmation dialog), not an alert or menu, for choices related to an action people initiated; anchor it to its source control, put destructive choices at the top, Cancel at the bottom, and avoid scrolling (watchOS: at most four buttons including Cancel).

rules.title: Keep popovers small and single
rules.rule: SHOULD use popovers for small amounts of related functionality, point them at their source, save work when they auto-close, never cascade them, never use them for warnings, and use a sheet instead in compact widths.

rules.title: Organize menus predictably
rules.rule: SHOULD label menu items with title-case verbs without articles, list frequent items first, group related items with separators, dim (not hide) unavailable items in regular menus, limit submenus to one level of about five items, and give icons to all items in a group or none.

rules.title: Context menus mirror the main UI
rules.rule: MUST make every context menu item available elsewhere in the main interface, and SHOULD keep context menus short and relevant, hide unavailable items, omit keyboard shortcuts, and list destructive items last with destructive styling.

rules.title: Use list accessories correctly
rules.rule: SHOULD use a disclosure indicator to drill into a row, an info (detail disclosure) button only to reveal more information, and no alphabetical index alongside trailing accessories.

rules.title: Don’t nest same-axis scroll views
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT place a scroll view inside another scroll view with the same orientation; horizontal-in-vertical (or the reverse) is fine.

rules.title: Secure sensitive text entry
rules.rule: MUST use a secure text field for passwords and other sensitive data, and MUST NOT prefill password fields.

rules.title: Configure text fields for their content
rules.rule: SHOULD show the keyboard type that matches the content, size fields to the expected text, stack multiple fields vertically with consistent widths and logical tab order, validate at the right moment, and offer a Clear button on iOS.

rules.title: Use switches only in list rows (iOS)
rules.rule: SHOULD use the switch toggle style only in list rows; elsewhere use a button that behaves like a toggle, and make on/off states differ by more than color.

rules.title: Keep segmented controls tight
rules.rule: SHOULD limit segmented controls to about five segments on iPhone (five to seven in wide layouts), keep segments equal in width, use text or images but not both, label with nouns, and never use them to switch app sections.

rules.title: Pick the right selection control
rules.rule: SHOULD use a pull-down button for short lists, a picker for medium-to-long lists with predictable ordering shown in context, and a list or table for very long lists.

rules.title: Sliders follow platform direction
rules.rule: MUST NOT use a slider for audio volume on iOS/iPadOS (use the system volume view); SHOULD put minimum values on the leading (or bottom) side and maximum on the trailing (or top) side.

rules.title: Report progress honestly
rules.rule: SHOULD prefer determinate progress, advance it accurately, keep indicators moving, use specific descriptions (not “Loading”), keep them in a consistent location, allow Cancel/Pause when safe, and never switch between a spinner and a bar.

rules.title: Let people copy useful labels
rules.rule: MAY make useful label text (error messages, addresses, IP addresses) selectable so people can copy it.

rules.title: Launch screens are not splash screens
rules.rule: MUST NOT advertise or brand on the launch screen; it SHOULD be nearly identical to the first screen, contain no text, and match the current orientation and appearance.

rules.title: Make onboarding fast, interactive, optional
rules.rule: SHOULD teach through interaction and contextual tips, keep required flows brief, make tutorials skippable and findable later, postpone nonessential setup, and ask for ratings or purchases only after people engage.

rules.title: Show something immediately
rules.rule: SHOULD show placeholder content right away while loading, let people keep working during loads, and download large assets in the background.

rules.title: Match feedback to significance
rules.rule: SHOULD integrate status feedback inline, warn only about unexpected and irreversible data loss, confirm only significant completions, explain why a command can’t run, and deliver feedback through more than one channel.

rules.title: Keep settings minimal and expected
rules.rule: SHOULD ship great defaults, minimize settings, open settings with ⌘, where a keyboard exists, detect information instead of asking for it, and put task-specific options in the task itself.

rules.title: Make undo predictable
rules.rule: SHOULD support multiple levels of undo and redo through system mechanisms, describe what will be undone (“Undo Typing”), and reveal the result even when it’s off screen.

rules.title: Minimize data entry
rules.rule: SHOULD gather information from the system when possible, offer choices instead of typing, support paste and drag and drop, validate as people type, and enable Next or Continue only when required data is present.

rules.title: Full screen stays in people’s control
rules.rule: SHOULD let people choose when to enter and exit full screen, keep essential controls reachable, let the Dock appear (except in games), and resume where people left off.

rules.title: Request permission in context
rules.rule: SHOULD request only the data a feature needs, at the moment people use that feature, and avoid launch-time requests unless the app can’t function without the data.

rules.title: Write specific purpose strings
rules.rule: SHOULD write each purpose string as one brief, specific, active sentence in sentence case ending with a period (“The app records during the night to detect snoring sounds.”).

rules.title: Pre-permission screens: one honest button
rules.rule: MUST NOT add actions other than a single “Continue” or “Next” button to a custom screen shown before a permission alert (no “Allow”, no cancel or close), unless required for legal consent.

rules.title: Never mislead before the tracking prompt
rules.rule: MUST NOT precede the App Tracking Transparency alert with screens that offer incentives, imitate a request, show an image of the alert, or annotate it — these cause App Review rejection.

rules.title: Use system authentication and secure storage
rules.rule: MUST NOT store passwords or secrets in plain text; SHOULD prefer passkeys, Sign in with Apple, Password AutoFill, and Face ID/Touch ID/Optic ID over custom schemes, and keep secrets in the keychain.

rules.title: Disclose AI; never impersonate humans
rules.rule: MUST NOT lead people to think they’re interacting with, or viewing content authored by, a human when it’s AI; clearly identify where the app uses AI and what it can and can’t do.

rules.title: Keep people in control of results
rules.rule: SHOULD let people dismiss, edit, undo, retry, or adjust generated content with controls near the result, and acknowledge when their corrections take effect.

rules.title: Confirm before significant actions
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT automate destructive or hard-to-undo actions (deleting data, purchases); ask for confirmation before acting on someone’s behalf.

rules.title: Protect privacy in AI features
rules.rule: SHOULD prefer on-device models, ask permission before using personal data, minimize and disclose what’s sent to servers or used for training, and offer a clear opt-out.

rules.title: Limit and disclose hallucination risk
rules.rule: SHOULD scope generation narrowly, avoid requesting facts the model can’t verify, communicate that AI output may contain errors, and avoid AI content where a mistake could cause harm.

rules.title: Design the waiting and fallback experience
rules.rule: SHOULD show specific progress messages (“Summarizing key themes from your notes”), consider offering alternative results, provide voluntary feedback controls, coach people when requests are blocked, and keep a non-AI fallback when possible.

rules.title: Standard gestures do standard things
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT use a familiar gesture (tap, swipe, drag) for an app-unique action, or invent a gesture for a standard action like activating a button or scrolling.

rules.title: Custom gestures are never the only way
rules.rule: MUST make custom gestures discoverable, easy to perform, distinct from other gestures, and never the only way to perform an important action; shortcut gestures supplement standard controls such as the Back button.

rules.title: Don’t collide with system gestures
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT define gestures that conflict with system gestures (three-finger undo/redo and copy/paste, shake to undo, iPad four-finger app switching, edge swipes, visionOS palm and hand-roll overlays).

rules.title: Respond to gestures immediately
rules.rule: SHOULD give immediate feedback during gestures and clearly indicate when a gesture isn’t available (for example, a locked object that can’t be dragged).

rules.title: Keep standard keyboard shortcuts
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT repurpose standard shortcuts (⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘X, ⌘Z, ⇧⌘Z, ⌘A, ⌘F, ⌘N, ⌘O, ⌘P, ⌘S, ⌘W, ⌘Q, ⌘, ⌘? and others); only reassign one whose action makes no sense in the app.

rules.title: Build custom shortcuts the Apple way
rules.rule: SHOULD add custom shortcuts only for frequent commands, use Command as the main modifier and Shift as secondary, use Option sparingly, avoid Control, list modifiers in the order Control, Option, Shift, Command, and not add Shift for a key’s upper character.

rules.title: Let the system own focus
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT move focus without people’s interaction (except when the focused item disappears during directional navigation); rely on system focus effects, using a focus ring for text fields and a highlight for list rows.

rules.title: tvOS: design for directional focus
rules.rule: SHOULD make every element reachable by directional focus, avoid a free pointer in menus, design all five focus states, and supply assets sized for the enlarged focused state.

rules.title: visionOS: indirect gestures first
rules.rule: SHOULD prefer indirect gestures (look and tap) for UI, reserve direct touch for nearby objects used briefly, avoid requiring specific body positions or a specific hand, and give interactive items rounded shapes with a single containing highlight region.

rules.title: watchOS: respect double tap
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT set a primary double-tap action in views with lists, scroll views, or vertical tabs; in nonscrolling views, assign it to the most-used button.

rules.title: iPadOS: keyboard navigation for content, not controls
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT add custom keyboard navigation to buttons, segmented controls, or switches; support it for text fields, text views, sidebars, and collections, and let Full Keyboard Access handle controls.

rules.title: Put frequent controls within reach
rules.rule: SHOULD place frequently used controls in the middle or bottom of the screen, limit on-screen controls, and support swipe to navigate back and swipe actions in list rows.

rules.title: Use device capabilities instead of data entry
rules.rule: SHOULD, with permission, use platform capabilities (Apple Pay, biometric authentication, location) rather than asking people to type information.

rules.title: Keep toolbar items clear of window controls
rules.rule: MUST make sure leading toolbar items move inward when windowed-mode window controls appear, so the controls never hide them.

rules.title: Every menu bar command is also in the UI
rules.rule: MUST ensure every function in the iPadOS menu bar (including dynamic menu items) is also reachable through the app’s interface, since the menu bar is hidden until revealed.

rules.title: Support fluid window resizing
rules.rule: SHOULD support arbitrary window sizes with split views that reflow fluidly, minimize modality and full-screen transitions, and size density to viewing distance and input mode.

rules.title: Build to resize
rules.rule: MUST lay out with size classes (compact on the outer display, regular on the inner), layout margins, and safe-area insets, with no fixed widths or display-specific dependencies.

rules.title: Same functionality across displays and poses
rules.rule: MUST keep functionality, element state, and access to controls the same across displays and device poses; MAY show one additional level of hierarchy on the inner display.

rules.title: Follow the system’s vertical controls
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT override the default side placement of toolbars, tab bars, and navigation controls; keep relative control positions consistent across poses and account for asymmetric content areas.

rules.title: Keep important content out of reserved regions
rules.rule: SHOULD keep important elements clear of the cameras and the folding region (using `ReservedRegion` for custom UI), prefer containers that adapt to the fold and even-numbered grid columns, and avoid extreme layout changes as the device folds.

rules.title: Configure toolbar items for the vertical axis
rules.rule: SHOULD give every non-text toolbar item both a title and a symbol, put Back/Close first then prominent actions, set visibility priorities, group items with system groups instead of manual spacing, and use the system overflow menu (reserving the ellipsis for it).

rules.title: Keep navigation outside arrangement views
rules.rule: SHOULD use arrangement views (split or overlay) for two-view layouts and place navigation containers around them, not inside.

rules.title: The menu bar holds every command
rules.rule: MUST list every app command in the menu bar in the standard order (App, File, Edit, Format, View, app-specific, Window, Help), always show the same items (disable rather than hide), and support standard shortcuts.

rules.title: Every toolbar item is also a menu command
rules.rule: MUST make every toolbar item available as a menu bar command, because people can customize or hide the toolbar.

rules.title: Use system windows and their states
rules.rule: MUST use system window frames and the system main/key/inactive appearances; let people resize, move, and take windows full screen; and keep critical information out of bottom bars.

rules.title: Follow settings window conventions
rules.rule: SHOULD open settings from the App menu’s Settings… item (⌘,), dim the minimize and zoom buttons, use a noncustomizable toolbar that shows the active pane, title the window with the pane name, and reopen the last pane.

rules.title: Menu bar extras stay optional
rules.rule: SHOULD represent a menu bar extra with a symbol, show a menu (not a popover) when clicked, let people decide whether to show it, and expose the same functionality elsewhere (e.g., a Dock menu).

rules.title: Embrace the focus system
rules.rule: SHOULD communicate focus with scale, parallax, and illumination — not color alone — and pad items so focused growth never overlaps content.

rules.title: Use layered images for the app icon
rules.rule: MUST use a layered image (two to five layers, opaque background layer) for the tvOS app icon, and SHOULD use layered images for other focusable artwork.

rules.title: Minimize typing and sign-in friction
rules.rule: SHOULD minimize text entry, make sign-in easy and infrequent, support shared sign-in and profile switching, and provide search suggestions.

rules.title: Choose the minimum immersion
rules.rule: SHOULD use windows for familiar UI, volumes for bounded 3D content, and immersive spaces only for moments that need them, launching in the Shared Space.

rules.title: Anchor content in space, not to the head
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT anchor content to the wearer’s head; keep important content centered in the field of view and support use with minimal physical movement.

rules.title: Size windows for their content
rules.rule: SHOULD pick an initial window size and shape that fits the content (default 1280×720 pt) with minimal empty space, set minimum and maximum sizes, and avoid opening too many windows.

rules.title: Use depth sparingly and never on text
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT add depth to text; use depth to communicate hierarchy on large, important elements only, with accurate visual cues.

rules.title: Keep bars where people expect them
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT create vertical toolbars or pull-down menus in toolbars; use the system bottom toolbar and vertical leading tab bar, ornaments for app controls, and adjacent windows (not ornaments) for supplemental content.

rules.title: Design for a glance
rules.rule: SHOULD support quick, single-screen interactions that finish in under a minute, with shallow navigation driven by the Digital Crown.

rules.title: Avoid loading indicators
rules.rule: SHOULD NOT show indeterminate loading indicators; display content immediately and notify people when longer tasks complete.

rules.title: Full-width primary buttons
rules.rule: SHOULD use full-width buttons for primary actions, equal heights for stacked and side-by-side buttons, and toolbar buttons for corner actions.

rules.title: Complications, notifications, independence
rules.rule: SHOULD provide useful complications and actionable notifications, and let the app function independently of iPhone.

rules.title: No settings bundle in the Settings app
rules.rule: MUST NOT rely on adding custom settings to the watchOS Settings app; place a few essential options at the bottom of the main view or in a More menu.

rules.title: No Apple trademarks in names or images
rules.rule: MUST NOT use Apple trademarks in an app name or images; follow Apple’s trademark guidelines.

rules.title: No replicas of Apple hardware
rules.rule: MUST NOT reproduce Apple hardware in app icons, custom symbols, or artwork; when Apple devices must appear, use only Apple Design Resources images or the SF Symbols that represent Apple products.

rules.title: Respect SF Symbols terms
rules.rule: MUST NOT use SF Symbols — or confusingly similar images — in app icons, logos, or any trademarked use, and MUST NOT customize symbols that depict Apple products or features.

rules.title: Never imitate system UI
rules.rule: MUST NOT build custom window chrome that replicates system windows or screens that imitate system permission or tracking alerts.

rules.title: Let branding defer to content
rules.rule: SHOULD express brand through voice, a judicious accent color, content-layer color, an optional custom headline font, and the app icon — not by displaying logos throughout the app or restyling familiar components beyond recognition.

rules.title: Apply the same rules on every stack
rules.rule: SHOULD apply every rule in this set whatever the implementation — SwiftUI, UIKit, AppKit, a web framework, or React Native — translating it through the stack’s own mechanism instead of dropping rules the stack makes harder.
rules.why: People judge the interface, not the framework; an app is only consistent across Apple devices if every build follows the same rules (SYNC-01).
rules.do: Map system colors to `tokens.css` variables or `PlatformColor`, text styles to `rem` styles or Dynamic Type ramps, and Reduce Motion to `prefers-reduced-motion` or `AccessibilityInfo`.
rules.dont: Skip safe areas, Dynamic Type, or labels because “it’s just a web app.”

rules.title: Keep SF Symbols inside apps for Apple platforms
rules.rule: MUST NOT ship SF Symbols — as exported SVGs, fonts, or images — in websites, web apps, or builds for non-Apple platforms; use an open-licensed icon set there. Apps running on Apple platforms, including React Native apps on iOS, may draw SF Symbols through the system.
rules.why: Apple licenses these system-provided images solely for developing apps for Apple-branded products that run on the system they were provided for (Xcode and Apple SDKs Agreement §2.10).
rules.do: Lucide (ISC), Phosphor (MIT), Heroicons (MIT), or Material Symbols (Apache 2.0) on the web; `SymbolView` with SF Symbols on iOS and Material Symbols elsewhere in React Native.

rules.title: Build web controls from native elements
rules.rule: SHOULD build web controls from native elements — `<button>`, `<a href>`, `<dialog>`, `<input>`, `<select>`, `popover` — and SHOULD NOT attach click handlers to `<div>` or `<span>` elements, which have no role, focus, or keyboard support.
rules.why: Native elements are the web’s system components: they bring the role VoiceOver announces, keyboard focus, and activation behavior for free (SYS-01, A11Y-03, A11Y-07).

rules.title: Meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast on the web
rules.rule: SHOULD meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast in web builds in addition to COL-06 — 4.5:1 for text below 24 px, or below 18.66 px when bold — using the increased-contrast variants of system colors for colored text where the default variants fall short.
rules.why: WCAG is the accessibility baseline for the web and is stricter than the HIG for small bold text; blue on white is 3.52:1, while the increased-contrast blue is 4.57:1.
rules.do: `color: var(--adl-accent-text)`; colored text on the page background or a list row.
rules.dont: Blue or red text on a gray fill in light mode.

rules.title: Generate every stack’s tokens from one source
rules.rule: SHOULD generate colors, text styles, and sizes for every stack in a product from one token source instead of maintaining parallel values per platform or framework.
rules.why: Hand-copied values drift, and drift breaks the cross-platform consistency people rely on (SYNC-03).
rules.do: Edit `tokens.json`, run `build_tokens.py`, and ship the generated `tokens.css`, `tokens.ts`, `tailwind.css`, and `tokens.native.ts`.

rules.title: Use native views in React Native
rules.rule: SHOULD use native views in React Native — the system tab bar and navigation stack, `Switch`, `Alert` and `ActionSheetIOS`, `PlatformColor`, and Dynamic Type ramps — instead of JavaScript re-creations of system components.
rules.why: Native views bring Liquid Glass, Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, and future system changes for free; look-alikes must re-create and maintain all of it (SYS-01).
rules.do: Expo Router native tabs; a native stack with `headerLargeTitleEnabled`.
rules.dont: A custom JavaScript tab bar styled to look like iOS.
